OPERATIONS ANALYTICS / CASE STUDY 01

Less waiting.
Better evidence.

What can two years of baggage data tell us about a better airport experience?

A quantitative study of Melbourne Airport’s four terminals, exploring where handling performance changed after automated scanners were introduced.

01 / THE QUESTION

The first bag is
part of the journey.

Passengers see a carousel. Analysts see a process with measurable differences.

The study examines daily average time until the first bag reaches the carousel and daily baggage volume. In the study scenario, T2 and T3 received automated scanners on 1 January 2019; T1 and T4 did not.

The challenge: separate the changes we can observe from the explanations we still need to test.

Academic case study based on a supplied research report. This is an independent portfolio project, with no claimed affiliation with Melbourne Airport.

Compare 2018 and 2019 at T2 and T3, checking time alongside workload.

03

What happened elsewhere?

Use T1 and T4 as context for changes without the new scanners.

04 / THE ANALYTICAL APPROACH

From observations
to defensible decisions.

Three research questions guide the statistical investigation.

01

Describe the system

Summarise time and volume across four terminals and two years. Compare centres, spread and distributions before interpreting change.

Reported tools: means, medians, SD, coefficients of variation, heatmaps, scatter plots and boxplots. Figure 16 gives N = 730 daily observations per terminal over the two-year period.

Exploratory analysis
02

Check the assumptions

Inspect whether the observations follow a normal distribution before choosing how to compare groups.

The report uses Shapiro–Wilk tests (reported p < .001) and Q–Q plots. A paired t-test requires checks on paired differences and a defensible pairing rule; testing each year's distribution alone does not establish those assumptions.

Statistical reasoning
03

Compare and interpret

Compare terminals, then compare years within terminals. Read the time changes alongside changes in baggage volume.

Reported tests: Kruskal–Wallis across terminals, paired t-tests for T2/T3 and year-based ANOVA for T1/T4. These are reported results, not independently rerun tests; the raw daily dataset was not supplied.

Hypothesis testing
04

Audit the conclusion

Check the tables against the narrative. Distinguish an observed improvement from a proven effect of automation.

The website recalculates percentage changes from Figure 1. It corrects the interpretation of t-statistics as time savings and flags the inconsistency between T1’s reported means and the narrative conclusion.

Evidence communication
05 / THE EVIDENCE

The result is only as good
as its interpretation.

Read what the report found, what it means, and what remains uncertain.

Open source tables ↗
ATerminals have different arrival-time distributions.Reported p < .001+

What the output says

Kruskal–Wallis: H = 2455.110, df = 3, p < .001. The reported follow-up comparisons show T3 vs T4 as the exception (p = .798).

How to read it

At least one terminal differs. The omnibus test does not establish which process causes the differences. The shown Tukey comparisons should be checked against a rank-based post hoc procedure with multiplicity adjustment.

Figures 16–18 · printed p. 20 · source tables PDF, page 3.

BT2 and T3 recorded lower times in 2019.10.9% / 12.3% lower+

What the output says

T2: t(364) = −42.829, p < .001. T3: t(364) = −47.002, p < .001. The mean time fell by 0.465 and 0.934 source units, respectively.

How to read it

The values 42.829 and 47.002 are t-statistics, not seconds saved. Lower time coincided with lower volume at T2 and higher volume at T3. Volume, schedules and staffing may help explain the changes.

Figures 1, 19–20 · printed pp. 5, 22 · source tables PDF, pages 1 and 4.

CT1 worsened; T4’s small change was inconclusive.Check the direction+

What the output says

T1 mean rose from 4.769 to 4.952 (+3.8%); reported F(1,728) = 182.682, p < .001. T4 mean fell from 7.170 to 7.137 (−0.5%); the section 3.3 output reports p = .088.

How to read it

T1’s displayed means show a longer arrival time, despite the narrative calling it an improvement. The T4-labelled discussion refers to tables incorrectly captioned T2. At a .05 threshold, p = .088 does not provide sufficient evidence of a change; it does not prove equivalence.

Figures 1, 22–25 · printed pp. 5, 25 · source tables PDF, pages 1 and 5.

A NOTE ON ANALYTICAL HONESTY

A before-and-after study identifies change. Establishing the cause takes more.

The original daily data and analysis files were not provided. This website visualises transcribed report summaries and reports the original statistical outputs. It does not claim to reproduce the tests or independently verify the historical scanner installation. Time units are retained as unspecified source units.

06 / WHAT I WOULD DO NEXT

Turn a finding
into a better decision.

Observed changes suggest where to investigate. A stronger follow-up would test whether the improvement holds under comparable conditions.

Take the summary data ↗
  1. 01

    Validate the measurement

    Confirm time units, definitions, missing days, daily pairing and the scanner rollout record.

  2. 02

    Account for the workload

    Model flight schedules, baggage volume, seasonality and staffing. T2’s lower workload matters when evaluating its lower time.

  3. 03

    Estimate the effect carefully

    Explore a difference-in-differences design with T1/T4 as potential comparison terminals, checking parallel pre-trends and other changes first.

  4. 04

    Monitor the passenger outcome

    Track median and high-percentile first-bag times, last-bag times and passenger waiting times. Averages alone can hide a poor experience.
